clue.text: Cycling home, finally stopping where they sell wine

indicators.note: something stopping a word plugs a gap inside it, so this letter sits within the other piece
a cycle carries the front letter round to the back, so the word's opening letter moves to its end

parts.note: an abode is a dwelling place

indicators.note: finally points at the very end of the word that follows it, keeping only its closing letter

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone riding a bike home makes a last stop at a place selling wine.
explanation.walkthrough: ABODE cycles to BODEA, and the G slips in before the final A to give BODEGA.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodega is a Spanish wine shop or cellar, and in the US a small corner grocery store.

clue.text: A time to seal off copper mine entrance

indicators.note: to seal something off is to close it in on both sides, so the outer letters wrap round the next piece

parts.note: taken as written
a copper is a policeman; DI is a Detective Inspector
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone takes a moment to block off the way into an old copper mine.
explanation.walkthrough: A and T together close round DI: A(DI)T. Copper looks like the metal mined, but here it is slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: An adit is a horizontal passage driven into a hillside as the way into a mine.

clue.text: No change in Washington — rarely guilty

parts.note: taken as written
a cent is a small coin of loose change in American money

explanation.surface: A political commentator laments that nothing ever changes in the US capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rarely' belongs to the definition: the word is a rare one, the opposite of innocent.
explanation.definitionFit: Nocent is an archaic, seldom-used adjective meaning harmful or culpable, the counterpart of innocent.

clue.text: Colours ultimately faded of course

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the last letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
an emphatic agreement

explanation.surface: Naturally the colours in a garment have faded in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyes are substances used to colour fabric, so the noun stands for colours applied to cloth.

clue.text: Ian still occasionally appearing in dock, curiously

indicators.note: appearing in something means showing up inside it, so these letters sit within the following word

parts.note: a quay is a dock or wharf

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of the words is kept

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: A man called Ian keeps oddly turning up at the docks, or in the dock at court.
explanation.walkthrough: The kept letters slip between the third and fourth letters of the harbour word.
explanation.definitionFit: Quaintly means in an odd, charmingly old-fashioned way, so it serves as an adverb for curiously.

clue.text: Runs into old PM around Teesside town

indicators.note: turned around, the prime minister's name is read from its last letter back to its first
going into something places these letters inside the other piece

parts.note: Theresa May, a former British prime minister
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A former prime minister bumps into someone on a trip around a northern town.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn the name round first, then the R goes in before its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarm is a small market town on the River Tees in the borough of Stockton-on-Tees, north-east England.

clue.text: Stoke are playing — the epitome of Englishness?

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are being toyed with and moved about

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Stoke City are on the pitch, which a fan might call the essence of English football.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoke is a Potteries city whose football club is Stoke City. The question mark flags the definition as an example: the oak is England's national tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The sturdy oak is England's emblematic tree, celebrated in 'Heart of Oak', so these trees typify Englishness.

clue.text: Partly swapped permanently bleating female, we hear — well done!

indicators.note: with its parts swapped, the two halves of the phrase change places, back half first

parts.note: for good means for ever

indicators.note: what we hear is a word as spoken, which is spelt differently from its sound

parts.note: a female sheep, which bleats

explanation.surface: A sheep that keeps bleating has its bits rearranged for good, and someone says well done.
explanation.walkthrough: FOR GOOD with its two words switched gives GOOD FOR.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an exclamation of congratulation, used just like a cheer of approval after an achievement.

clue.text: Mount, in turn, but a little awkwardly

indicators.note: in turn suggests turning back, so the pieces are read from the end towards the start

parts.note: bar means except, as but does in 'all but one'
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone climbs on a horse in their turn, but rather clumsily.
explanation.walkthrough: BAR A read backwards gives ARAB. 'Mount' looks like a verb but is a noun: a horse to ride. The tail 'little awkwardly' only dresses the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An Arab is a breed of horse, and a mount is any horse one rides.

clue.text: Let out to catch bug

parts.note: to net is to catch, as in a fishing net

indicators.note: out means disordered or not in place, so the word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone releases a net to trap an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' looks like the insect to be caught; it is the verb meaning annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: To nettle someone is to irritate or annoy them, which is what bugging them means.

clue.text: Flipping idiots! Man U player's unexplained marks on body

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word is read back to front

parts.note: gits is British slang for fools
Juan Mata, who played for Manchester United

explanation.surface: A football fan swears at fools over a United player's mysterious bruises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British curse but signals the reversal. Man U is Manchester United, a football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Stigmata are marks resembling Christ's crucifixion wounds that appear on a person's body without natural cause.

clue.text: One's book a little bit of poetry

parts.note: 'one is' said in the first person is 'I am'
B is an abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A poet describes their own book as a slim volume of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The speaker counts as 'one', so one's, read as one is, becomes I AM.
explanation.definitionFit: An iamb is a metrical foot of one unstressed then one stressed syllable, a tiny unit of verse.

clue.text: Violently assaults in Chelsea store?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a stock of Chelsea footwear, ankle-length slip-on styles

explanation.surface: Thugs attack people inside a shop in fashionable Chelsea.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea looks like the London district with its shops; a Chelsea is a kind of ankle footwear, so a store of them is a set of them. Boots is also a British chemist chain.
explanation.definitionFit: To boot someone is to kick them, and Chelsea boots are a classic style, so a collection fits the second sense.

clue.text: They hate spending money abroad — this grates

indicators.note: abroad means spread about or astray, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Travellers who resent paying out on holiday find it really irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: Tight-arse is coarse British slang for a stingy person.
explanation.definitionFit: Misers are reluctant to part with cash; the slang term describes people who are mean with money.

clue.text: School getting parent's letter

parts.note: a gam is a school or pod of whales
an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A school receives a note sent by a pupil's mother or father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' suggests a classroom, but it is a group of whales. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamma is the third character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Attacker not a motorcyclist?

indicators.note: not a tells us that a single letter A is left out of the word

parts.note: one who carries out a raid

explanation.surface: Was the assailant someone other than a biker?
explanation.walkthrough: RAIDER without its A leaves RIDER. The question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorcyclist is someone who rides a motorbike, one kind of person in the saddle.

clue.text: Old horny creature rolling round floor

indicators.note: rolling round turns the combined letters over so they run from back to front

parts.note: O is an abbreviation for old
a yak is a horned ox

explanation.surface: An aged horned beast rolls about on the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: O YAK backwards gives KAYO. 'Floor' is the verb: to knock down.
explanation.definitionFit: Kayo spells out KO, a knockout, and as a verb it means to knock someone down flat.

clue.text: Tots are busy with a balloon, perhaps

indicators.note: busy suggests bustling movement, so the letters are moved about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Small children are playing happily with a party balloon.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerostat is any lighter-than-air craft such as a balloon or airship; 'perhaps' marks the example.

clue.text: Michael gutted to stop doing jobs round the house? Clearly not

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so these letters fill the middle of the other piece
a gutted thing has had its insides removed, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: do-it-yourself home repairs
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Michael has been disembowelled to halt his home improvements.
explanation.walkthrough: DIY stands for do-it-yourself, the British term for amateur home repairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Dimly means faintly or obscurely, the opposite of seeing or explaining something with clarity.

clue.text: Party rubbish? He gets a woman

parts.note: a do is a social gathering
rot means nonsense
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man dismisses a party as nonsense, then wins a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorothea is a female given name, as in Dorothea Brooke of Middlemarch.

clue.text: Start to dredge North Yorkshire river — you may have to work at it

definitions.text: you may have to work at it

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter
the Esk flows through North Yorkshire to Whitby

explanation.surface: A council employee faces the hard task of clearing silt from a Yorkshire river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work at it' suggests effort on a task; it literally means sitting at the piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk is the table people sit and do their office work at, so the cryptic phrase literally describes it.

clue.text: Dross! Oscar unlikely for creaking old British drama

indicators.note: unlikely suggests something improbable or strange, so the letters come out in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic sneers that an old British TV show was rubbish and never going to win an Oscar.
explanation.walkthrough: Crossroads was a British TV soap opera set in a Midlands motel, notorious for wobbly sets and stilted acting.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running ITV soap was famously cheaply made, so creaking describes its rickety scenery and production.

clue.text: Mess in dish — language!

indicators.note: a mess is a jumble, so the following letters are muddled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook swears on spotting a mess in a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'language!' looks like a rebuke for swearing; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sindhi is an Indo-Aryan tongue spoken in the Sindh province of Pakistan and parts of India.

clue.text: Soldiers going round at speed

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so the outer letters wrap the next word

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
taken as written

explanation.surface: Troops are running at high velocity.
explanation.definitionFit: Rate means pace or velocity, as in travelling at a rate of knots.

clue.text: What can I earn in Bangkok? Say, that's capital

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the phrase out, using its sound rather than its spelling

parts.words: What can I earn in Bangkok?
parts.note: wages in Thailand, whose capital is Bangkok

explanation.surface: A job seeker asks about salaries in Thailand's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Bangkok looks like the capital being defined, but the answer is another Asian capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Taipei is the seat of government of Taiwan, its largest city, so it is defined plainly as a national chief city.

clue.text: Accompanied earl ordered guards around

parts.note: E is an abbreviation for earl

indicators.note: a guard surrounds what it protects, so this word wraps round the next piece

parts.note: put in order
c is short for circa, Latin for around

explanation.surface: A nobleman commanded his bodyguards to stay close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' looks like an anagram signal; it is SORTED, which holds C after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: To escort someone is to go along with them, so escorted means accompanied.

clue.text: Have to defend English poet

indicators.note: to defend something is to surround and protect it, so the outer letters enclose the next piece

parts.note: to own is to have
E is an abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone is obliged to stick up for an English writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have to' looks like 'must'; the words split, with 'to defend' doing the containing.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen was the English First World War poet who wrote 'Dulce et Decorum Est'.

clue.text: Attracted Prince — one extradited?

indicators.note: someone extradited is sent out of the country, so that word is taken out of the name

parts.note: Prince Andrew, the British royal
an is the indefinite article meaning one

explanation.surface: A royal drew attention: could he be one sent abroad for trial?
explanation.walkthrough: ANDREW losing AN leaves DREW.
explanation.definitionFit: Drew is the past tense of draw, which means pull or attract, as in drew a crowd.

clue.text: Doris's daughter dressed in red cuddling sweetheart

indicators.note: cuddling means holding in the arms, so the letters wrap round the next piece
dressed means arranged or put in order, so the letters are laid out anew

parts.note: taken as written
the heart of the word sweet, its middle letter

explanation.surface: A girl in a red dress hugs her boyfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Doris and Nereus had fifty sea-nymph daughters. The E sits inside NER-ID.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nereids were the sea-nymph daughters of the sea god Nereus and the Oceanid Doris.

clue.text: Tough outside but somewhat easier indoors

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of, so a stretch of the following words holds the letters

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Life is harsh out there, a bit gentler at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A rind is the hard outer skin of fruit or cheese, a tough exterior layer.

clue.text: Confuse extremists in Delaware

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the state's abbreviation

parts.note: DE is the postal abbreviation for the US state
the extremes of the alphabet, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Radicals in an American state sow bewilderment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' looks like militants; it means A to Z, the alphabet's two ends.
explanation.definitionFit: To daze someone is to stun or bewilder them so they cannot think clearly.

clue.text: Fair happening shortly — he's outside with dodgems at first

indicators.note: outside means on both sides, so this word wraps round the next piece
shortly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an event is something that happens
taken as written; the 's stands for is
and means together with

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: At a funfair, a man is out by the bumper cars first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' looks like the funfair in the surface but means just. Dodgems are fairground bumper cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Even-handed means impartial and treating everyone equally, which is what being just or fair involves.
